name: V60 – James Hoffmann Ultimate
description: ハリオV60ドリッパー。挽き目：中細挽き。

deep_dive.origin_story:
James Hoffmann published his "Ultimate V60 Technique" on YouTube in 2017, distilling years of competition experience and cafe consulting into a single, repeatable method. The video became one of the most-watched coffee tutorials ever, with over 15 million views.

The technique emphasizes a large bloom with a gentle swirl, followed by two main pours with intermittent swirling to ensure even extraction. Hoffmann designed it to be forgiving and consistent, removing much of the barista variance that plagues pour-over brewing.

creator.name: James Hoffmann
creator.bio: World Barista Champion 2007, author of "The World Atlas of Coffee," and one of the most influential figures in specialty coffee. His YouTube channel has millions of subscribers and has democratized coffee knowledge worldwide.

deep_dive.tasting_notes: Expect a clean, sweet cup with excellent clarity. The swirling technique promotes even extraction, producing a balanced body that highlights origin flavors. Acidity is bright but not overwhelming, with a smooth, lingering finish.
common_mistakes: Pouring too aggressively during the bloom, disturbing the coffee bed
Skipping the swirl after bloom — this is essential for even saturation
Using water that is not hot enough (Hoffmann recommends as hot as possible)
Grinding too coarse, leading to fast drawdown and under-extraction
Not waiting for the full bloom time before the first main pour
tips: Use water just off the boil (95–98°C) for light roasts
The swirl after each pour is gentle — think wine glass, not cocktail shaker
If drawdown exceeds 3:30, grind slightly coarser next time
Rinse your paper filter thoroughly to remove papery taste
Weigh everything — consistency is the key to this method

name: V60 – Tetsu Kasuya 4:6 Method
description: ハリオV60（粕谷モデル推奨）。挽き目：中粗挽き（標準V60より粗め）。

deep_dive.origin_story:
Tetsu Kasuya won the 2016 World Brewers Cup in Dublin with his revolutionary 4:6 method. The technique divides the total water into five pours: the first two (40%) control sweetness and acidity, while the last three (60%) control strength and body.

What made the method groundbreaking was its use of a significantly coarser grind than traditional V60 recipes. This counterintuitive approach, combined with the structured pour ratios, gave brewers a simple framework to dial in flavor profiles without changing grind size — just by adjusting the first two pour sizes.

creator.name: Tetsu Kasuya
creator.bio: Japanese barista and 2016 World Brewers Cup Champion. Founder of Philocoffea and known for his innovative, accessible approach to brewing science. His 4:6 method transformed how home brewers think about pour-over variables.

deep_dive.tasting_notes: The 4:6 method produces a well-rounded cup with adjustable character. With equal first two pours, expect a balanced sweetness-to-acidity ratio. The coarser grind gives a fuller body than typical V60 brews while maintaining good clarity. Finish is clean and medium-length.
common_mistakes: Grinding too fine — this method requires a noticeably coarser grind than standard V60
Not waiting for each pour to fully drain before starting the next
Pouring too fast, which undermines the controlled extraction
Forgetting that the first two pours are for flavor balance, not just wetting
Using the wrong total water ratio (should be 1:15, not 1:16.7)
tips: To increase sweetness, make the first pour larger than the second
To increase acidity/brightness, make the second pour larger than the first
Each of the last three pours should be equal in volume
Use a timer and scale — precision matters with this method
Try with single-origin light roasts to really taste the control this gives you

deep_dive.origin_story:
James Hoffmann's French Press technique challenged decades of conventional wisdom. Published on YouTube in 2016, he argued that the traditional 4-minute steep with a coarse grind was producing under-extracted, muddy coffee.

His method uses a finer grind, longer steep time (9+ minutes total), and crucially, never fully plunges the press. Instead, after removing the crust and scooping foam, the plunger sits just below the surface as a filter while pouring. This produces a dramatically cleaner cup than most people thought possible from a French Press.

creator.name: James Hoffmann
creator.bio: World Barista Champion 2007, author of "The World Atlas of Coffee," and one of the most influential figures in specialty coffee. His YouTube channel has millions of subscribers and has democratized coffee knowledge worldwide.

deep_dive.tasting_notes: Surprisingly clean for a French Press. The extended steep and lack of plunging produces a cup closer to a pour-over in clarity, but with the fuller body characteristic of immersion brewing. Expect rich sweetness, low bitterness, and minimal silt.
common_mistakes: Using a coarse grind out of habit — this method needs medium grind
Plunging the press all the way down, pushing fines into the cup
Not waiting the full steep time (patience is essential)
Stirring too vigorously when breaking the crust
Pouring from the press too quickly, disturbing the settled grounds
tips: After 4 minutes, gently break the crust with a spoon and scoop off foam
Wait at least 5 more minutes for fines to settle before pouring
Do NOT plunge — just rest the plunger on the surface as a strainer
Pour slowly and gently to leave sediment behind
This method works beautifully with specialty light roasts

name: AeroPress (Inverted Method)
description: AeroPress (flipped upside down). Grind: Medium-Fine.

deep_dive.origin_story:
The inverted method was developed by the AeroPress community in the late 2000s as a hack to solve a fundamental limitation of the standard method: premature dripping. In the standard orientation, water begins draining through the filter immediately, reducing control over steep time.

By flipping the AeroPress upside down (plunger on bottom, open end up), brewers could steep coffee like an immersion brewer and only filter when ready. This technique quickly became the dominant method in AeroPress competitions and among specialty coffee enthusiasts, despite inventor Alan Adler's original design intent.
deep_dive.tasting_notes: Fuller body than the standard method due to the true immersion steep. Expect a concentrated, espresso-like intensity with a clean finish thanks to the paper filter. Bright acidity with rich sweetness, and no grit or sediment.
common_mistakes: Not sealing the plunger properly, causing leaks when inverted
Overfilling the chamber, leading to spills during the flip
Flipping too quickly or carelessly — hot coffee can spill
Pressing too hard, which forces fines through the filter
Using too much water for the small chamber capacity
tips: Insert the plunger about 1cm to create a seal before adding coffee
Leave at least 1cm of headroom before flipping
Place your mug on top, grip both firmly, and flip in one confident motion
Press slowly and steadily — aim for 20–30 seconds of press time
Experiment with the metal filter for a richer, oilier cup

name: AeroPress – WAC 2025 Winner (Némo Pop)
description: AeroPress + Flow Control Filter Cap. Grind: Fine (Comandante 31 clicks, sifted at 200μm).

deep_dive.origin_story:
Némo Pop won the 2025 World AeroPress Championship with a meticulously engineered recipe that pushed the boundaries of AeroPress brewing. His technique combines an ultra-fine, sifted grind with the Flow Control Filter Cap to create a bypass-style brew with exceptional clarity.

The recipe uses a very concentrated brew ratio (1:5.5) with lower temperature water, then dilutes to drinking strength. By sifting the grounds at 200μm, Pop eliminated the finest particles that cause astringency while keeping the larger fines that contribute to body and sweetness.

creator.name: Némo Pop
creator.bio: 2025 World AeroPress Champion from France. Known for his scientific approach to brewing, incorporating particle size analysis and bypass brewing techniques into competition recipes.

deep_dive.tasting_notes: A remarkably clean and juicy cup with tea-like clarity. The bypass technique preserves delicate floral and fruit notes that would be lost in a full-immersion brew. Light body with vibrant acidity, complex sweetness, and an exceptionally long, sweet finish.
common_mistakes: Not sifting the grounds — the 200μm sieve is essential to this recipe
Using water that is too hot, which extracts unwanted bitterness
Forgetting the bypass dilution step after pressing
Using a standard filter cap instead of the Flow Control version
Pressing too fast through the fine grounds
tips: Invest in a set of sieving screens if you want to replicate competition results
The Flow Control Filter Cap restricts flow for a more even extraction
Dilute the concentrated brew to taste — start with a 1:1 ratio of brew to water
Use light-roasted, high-quality single-origin beans for best results
Temperature precision matters — use a gooseneck kettle with temperature control

name: AeroPress – WAC 2024 Winner (George Stanica)
description: AeroPress (Inverted at 4th mark). Grind: Medium-Fine (Comandante C40 58 clicks / 870μm).

deep_dive.origin_story:
George Stanica won the 2024 World AeroPress Championship in Tokyo with a complex, multi-step recipe that demonstrated extraordinary precision. His inverted method uses a high temperature (96°C) with a medium-fine grind and a concentrated ratio of 1:7.2.

The recipe features an elaborate 17-step process including multiple agitation phases, precise timing intervals, and careful temperature management. Stanica's approach showed that the AeroPress can produce competition-quality results rivaling expensive pour-over setups when pushed to its limits.

creator.name: George Stanica
creator.bio: Romanian barista and 2024 World AeroPress Champion. His winning recipe at the Tokyo championships showcased how precision and creativity can extract extraordinary flavors from the humble AeroPress.

deep_dive.tasting_notes: Intense and complex with a syrupy body. The high extraction temperature brings out deep caramel sweetness and stone fruit notes. Despite the concentrated ratio, the cup has remarkable balance with a smooth, coating mouthfeel and a long, sweet aftertaste.
common_mistakes: Rushing through the 17 steps — each timing interval matters
Not preheating the AeroPress and mug thoroughly
Using water below 96°C, which under-extracts at this grind size
Inconsistent agitation between steps
Not weighing each water addition precisely
tips: Practice the full sequence several times before expecting good results
Use a precise scale and timer — this recipe demands accuracy
The inverted position at the 4th mark gives optimal brew volume
High-quality, freshly roasted specialty beans are essential
Take notes on each attempt to refine your execution

name: Turkish Coffee (Traditional)
description: 銅のジェズヴェ（イブリック）。挽き目：極細挽き（パウダー状）。
grind_size_label: Extra Fine (powder, finer than espresso; like talcum)

deep_dive.origin_story:
Turkish coffee is one of the oldest known methods of preparing coffee, dating back to the 15th century in the Ottoman Empire. According to tradition, it was first brewed in Istanbul after coffee beans arrived from Yemen via Ethiopian traders.

The method was so central to Ottoman culture that it became part of marriage customs — a prospective bride would prepare Turkish coffee for her suitor, and her skill was considered a reflection of her character. In 2013, UNESCO inscribed Turkish coffee culture and tradition on the Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

The technique has remained virtually unchanged for over 500 years: extra-fine grounds are simmered (never boiled) in a cezve with water and often sugar, producing a thick, unfiltered brew with a distinctive foam (kaymak) on top.
deep_dive.tasting_notes: Intensely aromatic with a thick, almost syrupy body. The unfiltered grounds create a velvety mouthfeel. Expect deep chocolate and spice notes with low acidity. The foam (kaymak) adds a creamy texture. Traditional preparations with cardamom add a warm, exotic complexity. The grounds settle to the bottom, creating a residue used for fortune-telling (tasseography).
common_mistakes: Boiling the coffee — it should only foam up, never reach a rolling boil
Stirring after the initial mix, which disrupts foam formation
Using a grind that is too coarse — Turkish grind must be powder-fine
Rushing the process on high heat instead of slow, gentle heating
Serving without letting the grounds settle for 1–2 minutes
tips: Use cold water for the best foam development
Heat slowly on low flame — patience creates the best kaymak (foam)
Add sugar and spices (cardamom) at the beginning, with the water and coffee
Pour slowly to preserve the foam layer on top
Use a traditional copper cezve for the most authentic heat distribution
Never stir once heating begins — let the foam develop naturally

name: Turkish Coffee (Specialty / Competition)
description: Copper Cezve (handmade, thin-wall). Grind: Very Fine (between Turkish and espresso).

deep_dive.origin_story:
The specialty/competition approach to Turkish coffee emerged in the 2010s as third-wave coffee culture began reexamining traditional methods through a scientific lens. Competition brewers discovered that using a slightly coarser grind than traditional (very fine rather than extra fine), lower starting temperatures, and precise temperature curves could produce a remarkably clean and complex cup.

This modern take respects the heritage of Turkish coffee while applying contemporary brewing science: controlled agitation, precise temperature staging, and high-quality single-origin beans replace the traditional dark-roast blends and sugar-forward preparations.
deep_dive.tasting_notes: Cleaner and more nuanced than traditional Turkish coffee. Single-origin beans shine through with distinct fruit and floral notes. The body is still full and silky but with less sediment. Acidity is present and pleasant, a departure from the traditional flat profile. The foam is delicate and aromatic.
common_mistakes: Using too high a starting temperature — start with warm (60°C), not hot water
Grinding to traditional extra-fine rather than the slightly coarser competition grind
Over-agitating the brew, which increases bitterness
Using dark-roast commodity beans instead of specialty light-to-medium roasts
Not controlling the temperature curve during heating
tips: Start with water at 60°C and heat very slowly for maximum control
Use a thin-walled copper cezve for responsive heat transfer
Try omitting sugar to let the bean's natural sweetness come through
A slightly coarser grind than traditional gives more clarity
Use freshly roasted specialty-grade single-origin beans

name: AeroPress – James Hoffmann (Best Recipe)

deep_dive.origin_story:
After years of experimenting and making numerous AeroPress videos, James Hoffmann released what he considers his definitive "best" AeroPress recipe in 2023. The method is deliberately simple: standard (upright) position, fine-medium grind, and no agitation beyond the initial pour.

Hoffmann's approach strips away the complexity that competition recipes had added to AeroPress brewing. He found that the standard orientation actually produces a cleaner cup than inverted when combined with the right grind size and a higher water ratio. The recipe was designed to be foolproof and consistently delicious.

creator.name: James Hoffmann
creator.bio: World Barista Champion 2007, author of "The World Atlas of Coffee," and one of the most influential figures in specialty coffee. His YouTube channel has millions of subscribers and has democratized coffee knowledge worldwide.

deep_dive.tasting_notes: Clean, sweet, and incredibly approachable. The higher ratio (1:18) produces a lighter body than most AeroPress recipes but with excellent clarity and sweetness. Expect bright fruit acidity, floral notes from quality light roasts, and a smooth, tea-like finish.
common_mistakes: Grinding too coarse — this recipe needs finer than typical AeroPress grind
Adding unnecessary agitation or stirring
Using water that is not hot enough (use close to boiling)
Pressing too hard or too fast
Not letting the coffee steep long enough before pressing
tips: Keep it simple — the beauty of this recipe is its simplicity
Use water at 90–95°C for best results
Pour all the water at once, then wait 2 minutes before pressing
Press gently over 20–30 seconds
The standard (upright) position is intentional — trust the process

name: Scott Rao V60 Technique
description: Hario V60 Dripper. Grind: Medium-Fine.

deep_dive.origin_story:
Scott Rao's V60 technique, detailed in his influential book "Everything but Espresso" (2010) and refined through his consulting work, established many of the pour-over principles that later became industry standard. His method emphasizes a vigorous bloom, a single continuous pour in concentric circles, and the famous "Rao Spin" at the end.

The Rao Spin — a gentle swirl of the dripper after the final pour — became one of the most widely adopted techniques in specialty coffee. It ensures a flat, even coffee bed for uniform extraction and has been incorporated into countless other recipes. Rao's scientific approach to brewing variables helped transform pour-over from an artisan craft into a reproducible science.

creator.name: Scott Rao
creator.bio: Coffee consultant, author of "Everything but Espresso" and "The Coffee Roaster's Companion." One of the most influential voices in extraction science, Rao's work on even extraction, roast development, and brewing theory has shaped modern specialty coffee.

deep_dive.tasting_notes: Exceptionally even and balanced. The continuous pour and Rao Spin produce one of the most uniform extractions possible with a V60, resulting in a clean cup where every flavor is represented proportionally. Expect bright acidity, clear sweetness, and a silky body with no astringent or bitter notes.
common_mistakes: Pouring in a start-stop pattern rather than one continuous pour
Spinning too aggressively — the Rao Spin should be gentle
Pouring water directly onto the filter walls, bypassing the coffee bed
Not blooming aggressively enough in the first phase
Ignoring the importance of a flat coffee bed at the end
tips: After the bloom, pour in steady concentric circles from center outward and back
The Rao Spin: one gentle swirl after the last drop of water hits the bed
Aim for a completely flat coffee bed when drawdown finishes
If you see a dome or crater in the spent grounds, adjust your pour pattern
A gooseneck kettle with flow control is almost essential for this technique
